/-!
# Conjecture 9.53

by D. J. S. Robinson

Is the isomorphism problem soluble for finitely presented soluble groups of finite rank?

The isomorphism problem is *soluble* for a class $\mathfrak{X}$ of finitely presented groups if
there is an algorithm which, given two finite presentations of groups in $\mathfrak{X}$, halts
and decides whether the presented groups are isomorphic. Membership in $\mathfrak{X}$ is a
promise: nothing is required of the algorithm on presentations of groups outside
$\mathfrak{X}$, where it may answer arbitrarily or fail to halt. Accordingly the algorithm is
modelled as a partial recursive function (`Partrec₂`).

A group has *finite rank* (finite Prüfer rank, also called Mal'cev special rank) if there is an
integer $r$ such that every finitely generated subgroup can be generated by $r$ elements. For
finitely generated soluble groups this coincides with having finite abelian section rank and with
being minimax.

A finite presentation $\langle x_0, \dots, x_{n-1} \mid R \rangle$ is encoded by the number $n$
of generators together with a finite list of relators, each a word in the letters
$x_i^{\pm 1}$.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

theorem primrecPred_letter_lt :
    PrimrecPred fun p : ℕ × List (List (ℕ × Bool)) => ∀ w ∈ p.2, ∀ l ∈ w, l.1 < p.1 :=
  ((Primrec.nat_lt.comp₂ (Primrec.fst.comp₂ Primrec₂.left) Primrec₂.right).forall_mem_list
    |>.forall_mem_list).comp Primrec.snd Primrec.fst

justification.name: HasFinitePruferRank
justification.why_needed: Mathlib has the minimum generator count `Group.rank` only for one finitely generated group, but no predicate asserting a uniform bound over all finitely generated subgroups.

blocks.name: HasFinitePruferRank
blocks.text:
/-- A group has finite (Prüfer) rank if there is an integer $r$ such that every finitely
generated subgroup can be generated by $r$ elements. -/
def HasFinitePruferRank (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∃ r : ℕ, ∀ H : Subgroup G, H.FG →
    ∃ S : Finset G, S.card ≤ r ∧ Subgroup.closure (S : Set G) = H

@[category research open, AMS 3 20]
theorem kourovka.«9.53» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ f : FinitePresentation → FinitePresentation →. Bool, Partrec₂ f ∧
      ∀ P Q : FinitePresentation,
        IsSolvable P.PresentedGroup → HasFinitePruferRank P.PresentedGroup →
        IsSolvable Q.PresentedGroup → HasFinitePruferRank Q.PresentedGroup →
        ∃ b ∈ f P Q, (b = true ↔ Nonempty (P.PresentedGroup ≃* Q.PresentedGroup)) := by
  sorry

@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem hasFinitePruferRank_of_finite (G : Type*) [Group G] [Finite G] :
    HasFinitePruferRank G := by
  classical
  haveI := Fintype.ofFinite G
  refine ⟨Fintype.card G, fun H _ =>
    ⟨Finset.univ.filter (· ∈ H), Finset.card_filter_le _ _, ?_⟩⟩
  have : ((Finset.univ.filter (· ∈ H) : Finset G) : Set G) = H := by ext; simp
  rw [this, Subgroup.closure_eq]

@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem subsingleton_presentedGroup_of_numGenerators_eq_zero (P : FinitePresentation)
    (h : P.numGenerators = 0) : Subsingleton P.PresentedGroup := by
  have : IsEmpty (Fin P.numGenerators) := by rw [h]; infer_instance
  refine ⟨fun a b => ?_⟩
  obtain ⟨x, rfl⟩ := PresentedGroup.mk_surjective _ a
  obtain ⟨y, rfl⟩ := PresentedGroup.mk_surjective _ b
  rw [Subsingleton.elim x y]

claims.decomposer_note: Single yes/no decidability question (answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ algorithm): 'soluble' for the isomorphism problem means decidable, i.e. there is an algorithm (computable predicate on pairs of encoded finite presentations) which, for any two finite presentations promised to define soluble (= solvable) groups of finite rank, correctly decides whether the presented groups are isomorphic (a promise problem — behaviour on presentations outside the class is unconstrained, since class membership is itself undecidable); 'finite rank' is Robinson's finite Prüfer (Mal'cev special) rank — every finitely generated subgroup is r-generated for a fixed r — which for finitely generated soluble groups coincides with finite abelian section rank and with being minimax, so that reading is canonical; the polycyclic-by-finite case is solved (Segal / Baumslag–Cannonito–Robinson–Segal) but is not asked here and should not be added.
claims.reviewer_why: c02's declaration (partial recursive algorithm `Partrec₂ f`, correct and halting on every pair of presentations that both present soluble groups of finite Prüfer rank, unconstrained elsewhere) is the literal reading of 'the isomorphism problem is soluble for a class': the standard definition (Miller, Baumslag–Cannonito–Robinson–Segal, Even–Selman–Yacobi/Goldreich for promise problems without resource bounds) only asks for an algorithm that, given presentations of groups IN the class, halts with the correct answer. The six total-`Computable₂` candidates (c01, c03–c07) add a halting requirement off the promise; for promise problems this is strictly stronger (recursively inseparable c.e. sets give a partially-decidable promise problem with no total decider), and the solved special cases in the literature (Segal's polycyclic-by-finite algorithm, Grunewald–Segal for nilpotent groups) are proved only in the partial form, so the total reading could in principle assign the problem a different truth value than the notebook's notion. Edits to c02: replaced its long fold-based `PrimrecPred` proof with c07's one-line proof, renamed `HasFiniteRank` to `HasFinitePruferRank`, took c07's `hasFinitePruferRank_of_finite` test lemma and kept c02's zero-generator test lemma, expanded docstrings. All candidates agreed on Prüfer rank, Mathlib `IsSolvable`, `PresentedGroup`, `Nonempty (≃*)`, a single uniform algorithm, and the promise imposed on both inputs; c08 is c02's twin with an equivalent `Group.rank`-based rank definition and identity-reading of out-of-range letters.

decomposition_objections.text: Minor: the notes describe the algorithm as a 'computable predicate on pairs of encoded finite presentations' (suggesting a total function) while also saying behaviour outside the class is 'unconstrained'. These are not equivalent in general (a partial algorithm correct on the class need not have a total computable extension, since the class is neither c.e. nor co-c.e.). I followed the 'unconstrained' reading and the literature's usage by allowing a partial recursive algorithm that must halt only on the promise set; a reviewer preferring the total reading should replace `→. Bool, Partrec₂ f` by `→ Bool, Computable₂ f` and `∃ b ∈ f P Q, (b = true ↔ …)` by `(f P Q = true ↔ …)`.

/-!
# Conjecture 9.53

by D. J. S. Robinson

Is the isomorphism problem soluble for finitely presented soluble groups of finite rank?

The isomorphism problem is *soluble* for a class $\mathfrak{X}$ of finitely presented groups if
there is an algorithm which, given two finite presentations of groups in $\mathfrak{X}$, halts

A finite presentation $\langle x_0, \dots, x_{n-1} \mid R \rangle$ is encoded by the number $n$

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«9.53»

/-- A finite group presentation $\langle x_0, \dots, x_{n-1} \mid R \rangle$.
A letter `(i, b)` of a relator stands for $x_i$ if `b = true` and for $x_i^{-1}$ if
`b = false`, following the convention of `FreeGroup.mk`. -/
structure FinitePresentation where
  /-- The number $n$ of generators $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$. -/
  numGenerators : ℕ
  /-- The finite list of relators, each a word in the letters $x_i^{\pm 1}$. -/
  relators : List (List (ℕ × Bool))
  /-- Every letter of every relator refers to one of the generators. -/
  letter_lt : ∀ w ∈ relators, ∀ l ∈ w, l.1 < numGenerators

namespace FinitePresentation

/-- The condition that every letter of every relator refers to a generator is a primitive
recursive predicate on the raw data of a presentation. -/
@[category API, AMS 3 20]
theorem primrecPred_letter_lt :
    PrimrecPred fun p : ℕ × List (List (ℕ × Bool)) => ∀ w ∈ p.2, ∀ l ∈ w, l.1 < p.1 :=
  ((Primrec.nat_lt.comp₂ (Primrec.fst.comp₂ Primrec₂.left) Primrec₂.right).forall_mem_list
    |>.forall_mem_list).comp Primrec.snd Primrec.fst

/-- Finite presentations are finite data, so they can be fed to algorithms. -/
instance : Primcodable FinitePresentation :=
  haveI := Primcodable.subtype primrecPred_letter_lt
  Primcodable.ofEquiv
    {p : ℕ × List (List (ℕ × Bool)) // ∀ w ∈ p.2, ∀ l ∈ w, l.1 < p.1}
    { toFun := fun P => ⟨(P.numGenerators, P.relators), P.letter_lt⟩
      invFun := fun q => ⟨q.1.1, q.1.2, q.2⟩
      left_inv := fun _ => rfl
      right_inv := fun _ => rfl }

/-- The relators of `P`, as elements of the free group on the generators
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$. -/
def relatorSet (P : FinitePresentation) : Set (FreeGroup (Fin P.numGenerators)) :=
  {r | ∃ (w : List (ℕ × Bool)) (hw : w ∈ P.relators),
    r = FreeGroup.mk (w.pmap (fun l hl => (⟨l.1, hl⟩, l.2)) (P.letter_lt w hw))}

/-- The group $\langle x_0, \dots, x_{n-1} \mid R \rangle$ presented by `P`: the free group on
the generators modulo the normal closure of the relators. -/
abbrev PresentedGroup (P : FinitePresentation) : Type :=
  _root_.PresentedGroup P.relatorSet

end FinitePresentation

/-- A group has finite (Prüfer) rank if there is an integer $r$ such that every finitely
generated subgroup can be generated by $r$ elements. -/
def HasFinitePruferRank (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∃ r : ℕ, ∀ H : Subgroup G, H.FG →
    ∃ S : Finset G, S.card ≤ r ∧ Subgroup.closure (S : Set G) = H

/--
Is the isomorphism problem soluble for finitely presented soluble groups of finite rank?

That is, is there an algorithm which, given two finite presentations $P$ and $Q$ of soluble
groups of finite rank, halts with the answer `true` if the groups presented by $P$ and $Q$
are isomorphic and with the answer `false` otherwise? When $P$ or $Q$ does not present a
soluble group of finite rank, the algorithm may answer arbitrarily or fail to halt.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 20]
theorem kourovka.«9.53» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ f : FinitePresentation → FinitePresentation →. Bool, Partrec₂ f ∧
      ∀ P Q : FinitePresentation,
        IsSolvable P.PresentedGroup → HasFinitePruferRank P.PresentedGroup →
        IsSolvable Q.PresentedGroup → HasFinitePruferRank Q.PresentedGroup →
        ∃ b ∈ f P Q, (b = true ↔ Nonempty (P.PresentedGroup ≃* Q.PresentedGroup)) := by
  sorry

/-- A finite group has finite rank. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem hasFinitePruferRank_of_finite (G : Type*) [Group G] [Finite G] :
    HasFinitePruferRank G := by
  classical
  haveI := Fintype.ofFinite G
  refine ⟨Fintype.card G, fun H _ =>
    ⟨Finset.univ.filter (· ∈ H), Finset.card_filter_le _ _, ?_⟩⟩
  have : ((Finset.univ.filter (· ∈ H) : Finset G) : Set G) = H := by ext; simp
  rw [this, Subgroup.closure_eq]

/-- A presentation without generators presents the trivial group. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem subsingleton_presentedGroup_of_numGenerators_eq_zero (P : FinitePresentation)
    (h : P.numGenerators = 0) : Subsingleton P.PresentedGroup := by
  have : IsEmpty (Fin P.numGenerators) := by rw [h]; infer_instance
  refine ⟨fun a b => ?_⟩
  obtain ⟨x, rfl⟩ := PresentedGroup.mk_surjective _ a
  obtain ⟨y, rfl⟩ := PresentedGroup.mk_surjective _ b
  rw [Subsingleton.elim x y]

end Kourovka.«9.53»

items: 'Soluble isomorphism problem' is modelled as a promise problem with a PARTIAL recursive function (Partrec₂): on pairs of presentations that both present soluble groups of finite rank, f must halt and output true iff the groups are isomorphic; outside the promise f may output anything or fail to halt. This follows standard promise-problem semantics and matches how such algorithms are given in the literature (e.g. Segal's algorithm for polycyclic-by-finite groups does not halt on other inputs). A total Computable₂ version would be a stronger statement, not provably equivalent since the class is neither c.e. nor co-c.e.

'Finite rank' is Prüfer/Mal'cev rank: ∃ r, ∀ finitely generated subgroup H, ∃ S : Finset G with S.card ≤ r and Subgroup.closure S = H (as in the decomposition notes; equals finite abelian section rank / minimax for f.g. soluble groups).

A finite presentation is encoded as (n, list of relator words over ℕ × Bool) with the well-formedness condition that all indices are < n; the letter (i, true) is x_i and (i, false) is x_i⁻¹ (Mathlib's FreeGroup.mk convention). Relators form a List (order/repetition irrelevant to the group).
Isomorphism is Nonempty (P.PresentedGroup ≃* Q.PresentedGroup); 'soluble group' is Mathlib's IsSolvable.
The promise is imposed on P and Q separately (each presents a soluble group of finite rank), and the pair is passed to the algorithm; nothing is assumed about the polycyclic-by-finite case.

reviewer_notes: Single slot, shipped. Key interpretive point: total vs partial algorithm. The decomposition notes said 'computable predicate' but also 'behaviour outside the class is unconstrained'; these differ for promise problems (a partial decider on a promise set need not extend to a total computable function, e.g. effectively inseparable c.e. sets). I sided with c02/c08's objection and the group-theory literature's definition: the algorithm must halt and answer correctly on every pair of finite presentations of soluble groups of finite rank; off the promise it may answer arbitrarily or diverge. This is the weaker (implied-by-total) requirement and is the form in which the known positive results (polycyclic-by-finite, nilpotent) are actually established. A reviewer preferring the total reading can replace `→. Bool, Partrec₂ f` by `→ Bool, Computable₂ f` and `∃ b ∈ f P Q, (b = true ↔ …)` by `(f P Q = true ↔ …)`; this yields a strictly stronger positive claim. Other checks: 'finite rank' = finite Prüfer (Mal'cev special) rank, stated as ∃ r, every f.g. subgroup is generated by ≤ r elements (all candidates agreed; c08's `Group.rank ≤ r` form is equivalent). Finite presentations are encoded as (n, list of words over ℕ × Bool) with the validity condition that all indices are < n, with a Primcodable instance derived from a proved PrimrecPred (no axioms). FreeGroup.mk sign convention verified ((a,false) = (of a)⁻¹). Boundary: the zero-generator presentation is in the promise class (trivial group is soluble of finite rank), so the statement is not vacuous; the promise class contains non-isomorphic pairs (e.g. trivial group vs ℤ), so no constant algorithm works. The polycyclic-by-finite solved case was not added. c03/c05 flip the Bool sign convention (harmless, documented); c01 routes through a derived `Encodable` and an ℕ-coded algorithm (fine but less transparent). File compiles with only the `declaration uses 'sorry'` warning; all lines ≤ 100 chars; AMS tags 3 20 ascending.
